title: Energy: from fossil fuels to windmills

words.ex: On the Ustyurt plateau, an oil well that had been dry for years suddenly started producing again after engineers drilled deeper.
Local fishermen complain that the new offshore gas field has scared the fish away from their part of the sea.
The engineers live for two weeks at a time on the drilling platform, far out at sea, before flying home by helicopter.
Angren's coal-fired boilers kept the town warm for decades, but they also coated every windowsill in black dust.
When a fire broke out at the power station, half the town was left without electricity for a whole day.
My great-uncle worked underground in a coal mine for thirty years, and he still coughs from the dust.
Workers dug a long trench across the cotton fields to lay a pipeline that will finally bring gas to our village.
Building turbines onshore is cheaper than putting them out at sea, where cables and repairs cost far more.
On the drive across the steppe we passed a wind farm with dozens of white turbines turning slowly.
The shepherds put solar panels on the roof of their hut in the mountains, so they have light even though no cables reach it.
Below the dam, the rushing river turns the turbines of a small hydroelectric station that lights the whole valley.
Some farms burn biomass, such as cotton stalks and dried animal waste, to heat their greenhouses in winter.
Twice a day the sea rushes in and out of the narrow bay, so engineers plan to use tidal power there.
Engineers testing wave power anchor floating machines off the coast, where the rocking of the sea drives their generators.
Our town hopes to get half of its electricity from renewables such as sun and wind within ten years.
In the debate club, Laylo argued that nuclear power is cleaner than coal, while her opponent worried about radioactive waste.
The mountain spa heats its pools with geothermal energy, using hot water pumped up from deep underground.
Our family's energy consumption almost doubles in winter, when the heaters are on all day.
Air conditioners are power-hungry machines, so our school only switches them on during the hottest weeks of the year.
When Aunt Feruza moved into her new flat, she bought all the kitchen appliances at once: a fridge, a cooker and a dishwasher.
The TV still uses electricity on standby, so my sister switches it off at the wall every night.
Uncle Sardor finally sold his old gas-guzzler, which needed a full tank every three days.
The new energy-efficient bulbs in our classroom use far less electricity and last for years.
Buying apricots grown in the Fergana Valley rather than fruit flown in from abroad keeps the food miles low.
Taking the fast train to Samarkand instead of flying is an easy way to shrink your carbon footprint.
Geologists have found rich copper deposits under the hills, and a new mine will open there next year.
If the water in the village well runs out in August again, families will have to buy water from the tanker.
A single wind turbine on the hill behind the college produces enough electricity for all its classrooms.
Old fridges consume far more electricity than modern ones, so replacing them soon pays for itself.
Underground supplies of coal are finite, so sooner or later the mines in the region will have to close.
